Giuseppe Verdi. The dominant composer of nineteenth-century Italian opera and a national icon of the Italian unification movement known as the Risorgimento.

Verdi composed twenty-eight operas over his long career, refining the bel canto tradition into highly dramatic, character-driven works. Among his most famous masterpieces are Rigoletto, La traviata, Il trovatore, and the grand opera Aida. Later in life, he came out of retirement to write two Shakespearean masterpieces, Otello and Falstaff.

Italian patriots shouted the slogan Viva V.E.R.D.I. as a coded acronym supporting Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia, the future King of Italy. This shows how closely linked Verdi was to Italian unification patriotism.

Va, pensiero, the Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves, comes from his early opera Nabucco written in 1842. It became an unofficial anthem of Italian unification, expressing longing for a lost homeland.

Rigoletto from 1851 is a tragic opera about a hunchbacked court jester. It is famous for the lighthearted tenor aria La donna è mobile, meaning Woman is fickle.

La traviata from 1853 tells the story of the courtesan Violetta Valéry who dies of consumption. It contains famous numbers like the drinking song Libiamo ne' lieti calici.

Beyond opera, Verdi is celebrated for his dramatic and operatic Messa da Requiem, composed in 1874 to honor the writer Alessandro Manzoni. This monumental setting of the funeral mass is celebrated for its terrifying, brass-heavy Dies irae depicting the day of judgment.

Arrigo Boito was the poet and composer who persuaded Verdi out of retirement to write the librettos for his final masterpieces, Otello and Falstaff, works featuring continuous music throughout.

Verdi was born in the same year as Richard Wagner, 1813, and the two composers represented opposing German and Italian philosophies of late nineteenth-century opera. He is the preeminent Italian composer of the Romantic era.
